screens.title: Encapsulation and Access Modifiers
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter we focus on encapsulation, the practice of bundling data and the operations that act on it so an object protects its own state. Encapsulation limits who can read or change internal details, and makes code more modular and safer to evolve. A helpful analogy is a bank account: deposit and withdraw are public operations you can call, but the internal balance and ledger are private — they aren’t changed directly by outside code. You will also learn the practical C# tools for enforcing encapsulation: access modifiers like public, private, protected and internal, and properties with get and set accessors that act as controlled gates to a private backing field. For Unity workflows, we also cover the [SerializeField] attribute so designers can edit private fields in the Inspector without making those fields public in code. By the end of this lesson you’ll be able to choose sensible defaults for fields, expose safe public APIs, and avoid common mistakes like overusing public fields. Think about the last time a value was set from many places; how might controlled access have prevented bugs there?

Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Encapsulation and Access Modifiers
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Encapsulation and Access Modifiers

Learn how to hide internal state, expose controlled APIs with properties, and balance Unity editor workflows using [SerializeField].

Safe public API
Analogy

A bank account exposes deposit and withdraw methods, but the balance is private. Accessors enforce rules like non-negative balances.

Why it matters

Encapsulation reduces bugs, localizes validation logic, and makes refactoring safer because internal details are hidden from other code.

Explore Key Topics
Access Modifiers
Control who can see fields, methods, and properties.
Properties
Gates with get and set to validate or clamp values.
[SerializeField]
Expose private fields in the Unity Inspector without breaking encapsulation.
In this lesson
You will learn how to hide sensitive fields, use properties to validate input, and expose designer-friendly fields safely in Unity.
Key Idea

Treat fields as private implementation details and present a small, validated public surface through properties and methods.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: In this set of objectives we focus on practical skills you can apply immediately. First, you will be able to explain encapsulation as an OOP principle: why bundling data with methods prevents external code from corrupting internal state. For example, you should be able to describe a class that exposes operations but keeps its fields private, and why that makes maintenance easier. Second, you'll differentiate access modifiers like public, private and protected and state precisely what code can and cannot access each member. Third, you'll implement properties with get and set accessors in C# to add validation and side effects when a value changes. Finally, for Unity development you'll apply [SerializeField] to expose private fields to the Inspector while preserving encapsulation. Each objective links a coding practice to a concrete benefit, like preventing invalid values or enabling designers to tweak values safely. As you work through examples, notice common beginner mistakes so you can avoid them in your own projects.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practice & Misconceptions
screens.narratorSegment: This second objectives slide ties the learning goals to common mistakes and practical checks. You will practice refactoring public fields to private ones and exposing safe properties; this helps you spot code that allows invalid states. Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Learning Objectives

Practice & Misconceptions

Use these practice checkpoints and watch for mistakes while coding.

Practice: Refactor fields

Convert easy-to-access public fields into private fields with public properties, adding validation where needed. Try this on an Item class from the previous chapter.

Practice: Use [SerializeField]

Expose only designer-facing fields in the Inspector so tweaks remain safe and non-intrusive to other scripts.

Common mistake

Making fields public because it's faster; this makes validation scatter across many scripts and hides assumptions about valid ranges.

Best practice

Default fields to private. Use properties to validate. Use [SerializeField] for editor exposure without giving other scripts direct access.

screens.title: What is Encapsulation?
screens.narratorSegment: Encapsulation is the practice of grouping data and the methods that operate on that data into a single unit, usually a class, and deliberately hiding the internal details. The point is to prevent outside code from directly manipulating an object's private fields in ways that break invariants. For instance, consider a character's health value: without encapsulation any other script could set health to negative or to an absurdly high number. Encapsulation means the class keeps a private backing field and exposes only controlled operations — for example, a TakeDamage method or a Health property that checks and clamps values. This makes it possible to centralize the rules about what constitutes a valid state. A useful mental model is a sealed box with labeled buttons on the outside. The buttons represent methods and properties that perform checks and side effects. The sealed interior is the backing field and implementation details. Beginners often confuse encapsulation with mere organization; the difference is access control. Being organized helps, but encapsulation enforces boundaries that the compiler and language features respect. As a quick exercise, identify one field in your last script that was changed from many places and imagine wrapping it with a property that validates inputs — what rules would you add? That reflection highlights why encapsulation improves reliability and maintainability.

content.html:
Core Concept › What is Encapsulation?

Encapsulation

Bundle data with the methods that operate on it and restrict direct access to internal fields.

Why it matters
Protects invariants, centralizes validation, and reduces coupling between components.
Analogy
A sealed box with labeled buttons: external callers press buttons, internal wiring stays private.
Misconception
Organization alone is not enough; access control enforces behavior at compile time and runtime.
Concrete example

Imagine a player health field that must remain between 0 and maxHealth. Encapsulation ensures all updates pass through methods or properties that clamp values and trigger side effects like death events.

Key Takeaway

Treat fields as implementation details and expose a minimal, validated public surface for other code to use.

Try this

Pick a public field in your code and plan a property or method that would validate every change to it. What constraints will you enforce?

screens.title: Access Modifiers Overview
screens.narratorSegment: Access modifiers control which code can access a type or member. Public means a member is visible everywhere; use it for the intended public A P I of your class. Private hides members so only code inside the defining class can see them; this is the default for fields and a safe starting point. Protected extends visibility to derived classes, allowing subclasses to use or override behavior while still hiding details from unrelated code. Internal restricts access to the same assembly, which is relevant when you split code across projects or libraries. In Unity, assemblies often map to the same project, so internal is less commonly used, but it matters when creating reusable libraries. Choosing the right modifier matters because it creates a contract: public members must be stable and documented; private members can be changed freely. Developers often mistakenly mark fields public for convenience — that lets other scripts bypass validation and creates fragile dependencies. A practical rule is: start with private, provide public properties or methods that intentionally expose behavior, and only use protected when designing for inheritance. For Unity scripts, remember [SerializeField] can make a private field visible in the Inspector while keeping the C# access level private. Which members in your project should be stable public APIs versus changeable implementation details?

content.html:
Comparison › Access Modifiers Overview

Modifier cheat sheet

public
Accessible from any code. Use for stable API members like methods that other systems call.
private
Accessible only inside the class. Use for backing fields and implementation details.
protected
Visible in derived classes. Useful when designing extensible base classes.
internal
Visible within the same assembly. Use when splitting code into libraries or packages.

Practical guidance

  • Default fields to private and only expose what you intend other code to use.
  • Use properties for validation, not public fields.
  • Use protected when you design for inheritance; prefer composition otherwise.
  • Reserve internal for multi-project assemblies and library boundaries.
Common pitfall
Making fields public to access them from other scripts makes it hard to enforce invariants and understand who can change state.

screens.title: Why Public Fields Cause Problems
screens.narratorSegment: Let's look at a concrete example that shows why public fields can be dangerous. Imagine an Enemy class with a public integer health field. Any other script can set health directly to -500 or to an absurd number, bypassing logic that handles death, clamps values, or triggers effects. This scatters validation across the codebase and creates surprising bugs. The safer approach is to make the backing field private and expose a public property or controlled methods. Properties provide a single place to validate changes, clamp ranges, and trigger side effects like playing a death animation. When refactoring, replace direct field assignments with property writes and move validation into the property's setter. A common beginner misstep is leaving public fields because changing signatures in many scripts seems harder than refactoring. In practice, refactoring once to centralize checks saves far more debugging time. Below you will see a code snippet showing the bad pattern and the encapsulated pattern. Read the code, then imagine another script trying to set health to an invalid value. How would the property prevent that error? Why Public Fields Cause Problems means public fields let external code bypass validation; private backing fields plus properties centralize checks and side effects.. In practical terms, a concrete enemy class example that breaks encapsulation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Definition › Public Fields vs Encapsulation

Bad: public field

public class Enemy
{
    public int health; // BAD: directly modifiable by any code

    public void TakeDamage(int damageAmount)
    {
        health -= damageAmount;
        // No central validation here
    }
}

// Elsewhere:
Enemy goblin = new Enemy();
goblin.health = -500; // Invalid value, no checks

Good: property with private backing

public class Enemy
{
    private int _health; // private backing field

    public int Health
    {
        get { return _health; }
        set {
            if (value < 0) _health = 0;
            else if (value > 100) _health = 100;
            else _health = value;
        }
    }

    public void TakeDamage(int damageAmount)
    {
        Health -= damageAmount; // validation runs here
    }
}
Key Takeaway

Use properties to centralize validation and prevent invalid assignments from other scripts.

screens.title: Properties: get and set with validation
screens.narratorSegment: Properties let you present a field-like interface while running code when values are read or changed. A property with a getter and setter can return a value and validate incoming values. In C# you can implement a full property with a private backing field when you need custom logic, or use an auto-implemented property for simple storage. Consider an Enemy class that uses a private _health field and a public Health property. The setter clamps values, prevents negatives, and logs changes. This pattern centralizes validation so any code that assigns to Health goes through the same checks. A common misconception is that a property is just shorthand for a field; instead, treat it as the place to put domain rules, side effects like event triggers, and clamping. When performance is critical, understand that trivial properties have minimal overhead, but properties with heavy logic should be used judiciously. Now, try to identify where you would add logging or event triggers when a value crosses a threshold. That is where properties shine: adding behavior without changing callers. Properties: get and set with validation means use getters and setters to enforce domain rules, trigger side effects, and keep a consistent validation point for all assignments.. In practical terms, turn private fields into safe, observable state. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Process Flow › Properties: get & set

Property pattern

Place validation and side effects inside the property's set accessor so all assignments follow the same rules.

When to use full property
When you need validation, clamping, logging, or to raise events when values change.
When to use auto-property
When no extra logic is needed; keep syntax concise and clear.
private int _health;
public int Health
{
  get { return _health; }
  set {
    int old = _health;
    _health = Mathf.Clamp(value, 0, 100);
    if (_health != old) Debug.Log($"Health changed to {_health}");
  }
}
Misconception
Properties are not just nicer-looking fields; they are the right place for domain rules and side effects tied to state changes.

screens.title: Auto-implemented Properties and 'private set'
screens.narratorSegment: Auto-implemented properties provide a concise way to declare properties when no custom logic is necessary. For example, public string Name { get; set; } automatically creates a backing field for you. They are perfect for simple data carriers or DTO-like objects. A common pattern is to make the setter private so other code can read the property but only the defining class can modify it. For instance, public int Score { get; private set; } allows game systems to display the score but only the owning class can update it via methods like AddScore. This preserves encapsulation while keeping code terse. Beware: if you later need validation on assignment, you'll refactor the auto-property into a full property with a backing field. That's a simple change but good to anticipate. Beginners sometimes treat auto-properties as a free pass to avoid thinking about invariants. Use them when no validation is required, and prefer explicit properties when you need control. Consider where values should be set: during construction, inside methods, or by external scripts. Choose the setter visibility accordingly. In practical terms, simpler syntax for common cases and read-only external access. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Comparison › Auto-implemented Properties

Auto-property examples

public class Player
{
  public string PlayerName { get; set; }
  public int Score { get; private set; }

  public void AddScore(int points) {
    Score += points; // allowed inside the class
  }
}

When to prefer private set

  • Expose read-only state to UI or other systems while controlling updates internally.
  • Use constructors or methods to change the property so invariants are preserved.
  • Refactor to a full property when validation or side effects are needed.
Tip
When in doubt, start with private set and change to a full property if logic is required later.

screens.title: [SerializeField] and the Inspector
screens.narratorSegment: Unity introduces a practical need: designers and artists must often tweak values in the Inspector, but making fields public just so they appear there breaks encapsulation. The [SerializeField] attribute solves this by telling Unity to serialize and show a private field in the Inspector while the field remains private in C# terms. This preserves the language-level access control while giving the editor visibility. For example, marking a private float movementSpeed with [SerializeField] lets a designer tune the value, but other scripts still cannot set movementSpeed directly. When you use [SerializeField], consider whether the field represents a static configuration value or runtime state; only serialized fields get their values saved with scenes or prefabs. A common misunderstanding is believing [SerializeField] makes a field public — it does not. Another important point: properties are not serialized by Unity by default; use a private serialized field for Inspector exposure and a public property to provide controlled access at runtime. This pattern keeps editor convenience and code safety both intact. In practical terms, expose private fields to designers without making them public. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Unity Integration › [SerializeField] and the Inspector

Serialize field example

using UnityEngine;

public class PlayerController : MonoBehaviour
{
    [SerializeField] private float movementSpeed = 5f; // visible in Inspector
    private int currentHealth; // not visible

    public int CurrentHealth {
      get { return currentHealth; }
      private set { currentHealth = Mathf.Clamp(value, 0, 100); }
    }
}

Guidelines

  • Use [SerializeField] for designer-tunable defaults and configuration.
  • Keep runtime state private and expose safe properties to other scripts.
  • Remember properties are not serialized; pair a private serialized field with a public property when needed.
Misconception
[SerializeField] does not change C# access levels; it only instructs Unity to serialize the field for the editor.

screens.title: Refactor an Item Class for Encapsulation
screens.narratorSegment: This walkthrough shows the practical steps to refactor an Item class to follow encapsulation rules. Start by making public fields private; this immediately prevents other scripts from modifying them directly. Next, add [SerializeField] to those fields that designers need to tune in the Inspector, such as itemName or itemWeight. Then create public properties: a read/write property for itemName, a read-only-from-outside property for itemWeight using a private set, and a public read-only property for IsStackable. Use the property setters to validate inputs, for example clamping weight to non-negative values and replacing empty names with a default. Update constructors and any methods to use the new properties instead of accessing fields directly. Finally, run your game and adjust values in the Inspector; verify that attempting to set invalid values via scripts is now prevented by compile-time access or by the property's validation. The key here is to centralize rules so that any change to the field must pass through the same validation logic. content.html:
Hands-on Activity › Refactor Item Class

Step-by-step

  1. Change public fields to private backing fields.
  2. Add [SerializeField] to fields designers should edit.
  3. Create public properties with validation and private setters where appropriate.
  4. Update constructor and methods to use properties.
  5. Test behavior in the editor and via code to confirm invariants hold.

Code template

public class Item
{
  [SerializeField] private string _itemName;
  private string _itemDescription;
  [SerializeField] private float _itemWeight;
  private bool _isStackable;

  public string ItemName {
    get { return _itemName; }
    set { _itemName = string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(value) ? "Unnamed Item" : value; }
  }

  public float ItemWeight {
    get { return _itemWeight; }
    private set { _itemWeight = Math.Max(0, value); }
  }

  public bool IsStackable { get { return _isStackable; } }

  public Item(string name, string description, float weight, bool stackable) {
    ItemName = name; ItemDescription = description; ItemWeight = weight; _isStackable = stackable;
  }
}
Key Takeaway

Refactoring once to encapsulate fields centralizes validation and prevents future bugs caused by uncontrolled assignments.

screens.title: Designing a Safe Public Interface
screens.narratorSegment: When designing a class A P I, prefer exposing behavior through methods and properties rather than granting direct access to internal data. Think in verbs: provide methods like Heal, TakeDamage, or ApplyBuff, which encapsulate the rule set for how state changes. A public property that returns computed values is acceptable, but avoid exposing mutable collections or raw fields that invite external code to mutate internal structures. If you must expose a collection, return a read-only copy or an interface that prevents modification. Another guideline is to make invariants explicit: if HP must be between zero and maxHP, enforce that in every entry point and document it in the A P I. Keep side effects predictable; for instance, have the setter of a property update internal state and raise events rather than let external scripts perform those steps separately. Designing a safe public interface reduces bugs and makes unit testing straightforward because you control the points where state changes. As you review your codebase, ask whether each public member is necessary, documented, and stable. If a member is only used by internal helpers, make it private.

Best Practices › Designing a Safe Public Interface

Expose behavior, not raw data

  • Provide methods that encapsulate rules (Heal, TakeDamage) rather than letting external code set fields.
  • Return read-only views for collections to avoid external mutation.
  • Document invariants and enforce them in properties and methods.
Example

Pro tip
Favor small public surfaces and guardrails. It’s easier to maintain and test stable APIs.

screens.title: protected and internal — when to allow derived access
screens.narratorSegment: Protected grants visibility to a member inside its declaring class and any subclasses. Use protected sparingly as a design choice: it is useful when you design a base class specifically to be extended and you want derived classes to access or modify certain internals. For example, a base Character class might expose a protected ApplyDamage method that derived Enemy or NPC classes can call or override. However, protected members create a tighter coupling between base and derived classes and can make refactoring harder because subclasses may rely on those internals. Internal limits visibility to the same assembly and is important when you split code into multiple projects or packages. In Unity projects that use the default single assembly, internal may be less relevant, but it becomes valuable when you create utility libraries or runtime packages. Protected & Internal › Design for extension

protected

Allows subclasses to access members. Good for intended extensibility points, not general exposure.

Example
protected void ApplyDamage(int amount) { ... }

internal

Visible within an assembly. Use for library internals or when grouping related code that should work together but not be public API.

Note
In many Unity projects, everything is in one assembly so internal behaves like public within the project. For packages, internal boundaries matter more.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and How to Fix Them
screens.narratorSegment: Beginners often default to making fields public for convenience, which quickly leads to brittle dependencies. Another common error is exposing mutable collections publicly, enabling external code to add or remove items without the owning class enforcing rules. A third mistake is relying on inspector tweaks to correct invalid runtime values rather than building validation into setters or initialization logic. To fix these, follow a few patterns: make fields private, expose read-only properties or methods, wrap collections with IReadOnlyList or return defensive copies, and centralize validation in properties or constructor logic. For Unity-specific issues, prefer [SerializeField] for designer-facing fields and keep runtime state private. If you need designer tools to change behavior at runtime, provide public methods that perform validation and update state appropriately rather than exposing fields. Finally, adopt small, tested public APIs and document invariants so other team members know the intended usage. These practical fixes transform code from fragile to maintainable. Common Mistakes › Fix patterns
Problem: Public fields
Replace with private fields and public properties with validation.
Problem: Mutable collections
Return IReadOnlyList or a defensive copy and provide methods to modify the collection with checks.

Use [SerializeField] for editor defaults and validate values on Awake or Start so runtime invariants hold.

  • Default to private fields.
  • Expose only necessary public methods or properties.
  • Centralize validation in setters or constructors.

screens.title: Key Concepts

This set of habits will make your codebase more robust, easier to test, and less likely to produce subtle runtime bugs.

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter we focus on encapsulation, the practice of bundling data and the operations that act on it so an object protects its own state. Encapsulation limits who can read or change internal details, and makes code more modular and safer to evolve. A helpful analogy is a bank account: deposit and withdraw are public operations you can call, but the internal balance and ledger are private — they aren’t changed directly by outside code. You will also learn the practical C# tools for enforcing encapsulation: access modifiers like public, private, protected and internal, and properties with get and set accessors that act as controlled gates to a private backing field. For Unity workflows, we also cover the [SerializeField] attribute so designers can edit private fields in the Inspector without making those fields public in code. By the end of this lesson you’ll be able to choose sensible defaults for fields, expose safe public APIs, and avoid common mistakes like overusing public fields. Think about the last time a value was set from many places; how might controlled access have prevented bugs there?

In this set of objectives we focus on practical skills you can apply immediately. First, you will be able to explain encapsulation as an OOP principle: why bundling data with methods prevents external code from corrupting internal state. For example, you should be able to describe a class that exposes operations but keeps its fields private, and why that makes maintenance easier. Second, you'll differentiate access modifiers like public, private and protected and state precisely what code can and cannot access each member. Third, you'll implement properties with get and set accessors in C# to add validation and side effects when a value changes. Finally, for Unity development you'll apply [SerializeField] to expose private fields to the Inspector while preserving encapsulation. Each objective links a coding practice to a concrete benefit, like preventing invalid values or enabling designers to tweak values safely. As you work through examples, notice common beginner mistakes so you can avoid them in your own projects.

This second objectives slide ties the learning goals to common mistakes and practical checks. You will practice refactoring public fields to private ones and exposing safe properties; this helps you spot code that allows invalid states. You will also apply [SerializeField] selectively so Unity designers can edit defaults while runtime code still controls state. A frequent misconception is that making everything public is faster; in reality it trades short-term convenience for long-term bugs and brittle dependencies. Another confusion is thinking properties are only syntax sugar; properties are the place to add validation, side effects like logging, or clamping logic. As you practice, adopt the rule: default to private, expose intention through public methods or properties, and only open visibility when you intentionally design an A P I surface. These habits will make your game systems easier to test and safer to integrate.

Encapsulation is the practice of grouping data and the methods that operate on that data into a single unit, usually a class, and deliberately hiding the internal details. The point is to prevent outside code from directly manipulating an object's private fields in ways that break invariants. For instance, consider a character's health value: without encapsulation any other script could set health to negative or to an absurdly high number. Encapsulation means the class keeps a private backing field and exposes only controlled operations — for example, a TakeDamage method or a Health property that checks and clamps values. This makes it possible to centralize the rules about what constitutes a valid state. A useful mental model is a sealed box with labeled buttons on the outside. The buttons represent methods and properties that perform checks and side effects. The sealed interior is the backing field and implementation details. Beginners often confuse encapsulation with mere organization; the difference is access control. Being organized helps, but encapsulation enforces boundaries that the compiler and language features respect. As a quick exercise, identify one field in your last script that was changed from many places and imagine wrapping it with a property that validates inputs — what rules would you add? That reflection highlights why encapsulation improves reliability and maintainability.

Access modifiers control which code can access a type or member. Public means a member is visible everywhere; use it for the intended public A P I of your class. Private hides members so only code inside the defining class can see them; this is the default for fields and a safe starting point. Protected extends visibility to derived classes, allowing subclasses to use or override behavior while still hiding details from unrelated code. Internal restricts access to the same assembly, which is relevant when you split code across projects or libraries. In Unity, assemblies often map to the same project, so internal is less commonly used, but it matters when creating reusable libraries. Choosing the right modifier matters because it creates a contract: public members must be stable and documented; private members can be changed freely. Developers often mistakenly mark fields public for convenience — that lets other scripts bypass validation and creates fragile dependencies. A practical rule is: start with private, provide public properties or methods that intentionally expose behavior, and only use protected when designing for inheritance. For Unity scripts, remember [SerializeField] can make a private field visible in the Inspector while keeping the C# access level private. Which members in your project should be stable public APIs versus changeable implementation details?

Let's look at a concrete example that shows why public fields can be dangerous. Imagine an Enemy class with a public integer health field. Any other script can set health directly to -500 or to an absurd number, bypassing logic that handles death, clamps values, or triggers effects. This scatters validation across the codebase and creates surprising bugs. The safer approach is to make the backing field private and expose a public property or controlled methods. Properties provide a single place to validate changes, clamp ranges, and trigger side effects like playing a death animation. When refactoring, replace direct field assignments with property writes and move validation into the property's setter. Let's summarize the essential concepts you should take away. Encapsulation means bundling data with the methods that operate on it and limiting direct access to internal state. Access modifiers control visibility: public exposes a member everywhere, private restricts it to the defining class, protected allows derived classes, and internal limits visibility to the same assembly. Properties with get and set accessors provide controlled access to private backing fields and are the right place to enforce validation and trigger side effects. Auto-implemented properties are concise for simple storage, and private setters are useful when you want public read access but internal write control. In Unity, [SerializeField] exposes private fields to the Inspector without changing C# access levels, keeping editor convenience and code safety both intact. Practice the rule: default to private, expose behaviour and validated properties intentionally, and use [SerializeField] for designer-configurable defaults. This set of habits will make your codebase more robust, easier to test, and less likely to produce subtle runtime bugs.

Second, use properties with get and set accessors as the central place for validation, clamping, and side effects like logging or events. Properties are where domain rules belong. Third, in Unity use [SerializeField] to let designers edit defaults in the Inspector while keeping fields private in C# so other scripts cannot bypass your validation.
